### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. hyperproinsulinemia  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.784)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:6081)

**Proposed mechanism:** Pathogenic variant in INS (null) —DISRUPTS→ INS (HGNC:6081); INS (HGNC:6081) —DECREASES→ Proinsulin (CHEBI:17790); Proinsulin (CHEBI:17790) —DISRUPTS→ Insulin processing and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-169988); Insulin processing and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-169988) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000831); Insulin processing and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-169988) —LEADS_TO→ Hyperproinsulinemia (HP:0011801). Pathogenic variants in the INS gene lead to impaired insulin processing and secretion, causing both diabetes mellitus (characteristic of Wolfram syndrome) and hyperproinsulinemia due to the accumulation of uncleaved proinsulin.

**How to falsify it:** The presence of pathogenic variants in the INS gene with a minor allele frequency > 0.01 in gnomAD would falsify the claim that these variants are causal for rare disease phenotypes. _(variant: null)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared genetic basis in INS can inform therapeutic strategies for both conditions, potentially involving insulin replacement or therapies aimed at improving insulin processing and secretion.

---

#### 2. diabetes mellitus, permanent neonatal 4  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.782)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:6081)

**Proposed mechanism:** INS (HGNC:6081) —PRODUCES→ Insulin (UniProtKB:P01308); Insulin (UniProtKB:P01308) —DISRUPTS→ Glucose Homeostasis (GO:0001975); Glucose Homeostasis (GO:0001975) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes Mellitus (HP:0000821). Loss-of-function mutations in the INS gene lead to reduced production or impaired function of insulin. This disruption of insulin negatively impacts glucose homeostasis, ultimately resulting in diabetes mellitus in both conditions.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in INS leading to gain-of-function mutations or identification of distinct causal genes for each disease that do not converge on insulin production or glucose homeostasis. _(variant: rs121912657)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared genetic and mechanistic basis of these neonatal diabetes subtypes can inform therapeutic strategies, potentially including insulin therapy or gene therapy approaches targeting the INS gene.

---

#### 3. type 1 diabetes mellitus 2  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.718)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:6081)

**Proposed mechanism:** Loss-of-function variants in INS (null) —DISRUPTS→ INS (HGNC:6081); INS (HGNC:6081) —DISRUPTS→ Insulin synthesis and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-165015); Insulin synthesis and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-165015) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000834); Insulin synthesis and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-165015) —LEADS_TO→ Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (HP:0005973); Insulin synthesis and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-165015) —LEADS_TO→ Wolfram syndrome (HP:0011753). Loss-of-function mutations in the INS gene disrupt normal insulin synthesis and secretion, leading to both diabetes mellitus (type 1 diabetes) and the broader phenotype of Wolfram syndrome.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of individuals with pathogenic loss-of-function variants in INS who do not present with either diabetes mellitus or Wolfram syndrome, or demonstration that the variants associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus 2 and Wolfram syndrome 1 affect distinct pathways downstream of INS. _(variant: The presence of common benign variants in INS within gnomAD that do not cause either disease would support the specificity of rare pathogenic variants.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared genetic basis of Wolfram syndrome 1 and type 1 diabetes mellitus 2 can inform therapeutic strategies targeting insulin production or function, potentially benefiting patients with either condition.

---

#### 4. obesity due to prohormone convertase I deficiency  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.427)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-264876)

**Proposed mechanism:** Loss-of-function variant in PCSK1 —DISRUPTS→ PCSK1 (HGNC:9024); PCSK1 (HGNC:9024) —DISRUPTS→ Prohormone Processing; Prohormone Processing —LEADS_TO→ Impaired processing of proinsulin; Impaired processing of proinsulin —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes Mellitus (HP:0000821); Prohormone Processing —LEADS_TO→ Impaired processing of POMC; Impaired processing of POMC —LEADS_TO→ Obesity (HP:0005101). Loss-of-function variants in PCSK1 lead to impaired processing of prohormones. Specifically, the cleavage of proinsulin into mature insulin is disrupted, contributing to diabetes. Concurrently, the processing of proopiomelanocortin (POMC) into active peptides like alpha-MSH is also affected, leading to dysregulation of appetite and contributing to obesity.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of individuals with MONDO:0013240 carrying homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in PCSK1 who do not exhibit any signs of obesity, or conversely, individuals with obesity due to prohormone convertase 1 deficiency (MONDO:0010961) who do not have impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes. _(variant: A common (e.g., >1% allele frequency in relevant populations) homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function variant in PCSK1 found in gnomAD.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of PCSK1 in processing critical metabolic hormones offers a potential therapeutic target. Modulating PCSK1 activity or its downstream effectors could offer a unified approach to treating both diabetes and obesity associated with PCSK1 deficiency.

#### 5. Cole-Carpenter syndrome 1  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.422)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-264876)

**Proposed mechanism:** P4HB (HGNC:8721) —DISRUPTS→ Protein folding and disulfide bond formation (GO:0006457); Protein folding and disulfide bond formation (GO:0006457) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal skeletal morphology (HP:0000924); Protein folding and disulfide bond formation (GO:0006457) —LEADS_TO→ Dwarfism (HP:0004303). Loss-of-function mutations in P4HB disrupt its role in protein folding and disulfide bond formation, leading to the accumulation of misfolded proteins and subsequent abnormal skeletal morphology and dwarfism in both MONDO:0013240 and Cole-Carpenter syndrome 1.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of individuals with pathogenic variants in P4HB who do not exhibit skeletal abnormalities or dwarfism, or finding that different genes entirely cause one of the diseases. _(variant: A common variant (AF > 0.01) in HGNC:8721 found in gnomAD that is shown to be benign.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of P4HB in protein homeostasis offers potential therapeutic targets for both conditions, possibly through chaperone therapy or strategies to enhance protein folding efficiency.

#### 6. neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and autistic features with or without hyperkinetic movements  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.396)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-264876)

**Proposed mechanism:** INS (HGNC:6042) —DISRUPTS→ neurotransmitter release (GO:0001722); VAMP2 (HGNC:12424) —DISRUPTS→ neurotransmitter release (GO:0001722); neurotransmitter release (GO:0001722) —LEADS_TO→ hyperinsulinism (HP:0000835); neurotransmitter release (GO:0001722) —LEADS_TO→ autistic features (HP:0000716); neurotransmitter release (GO:0001722) —LEADS_TO→ hypotonia (HP:0001252). Loss-of-function mutations in INS (causative for MONDO:0013240) and VAMP2 (causative for neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and autistic features with or without hyperkinetic movements) both converge on disrupting the essential process of neurotransmitter release, leading to overlapping phenotypic consequences such as hyperinsulinism, autistic features, and hypotonia.

**How to falsify it:** The hypothesis would be falsified if mutations in INS or VAMP2 are shown to have completely distinct downstream effects on neurotransmitter release pathways, or if the identified phenotypes for each disease are demonstrated to arise from entirely independent molecular mechanisms not involving neurotransmitter release. _(variant: gnomAD allele frequency > 0.01 for loss-of-function variants in INS or VAMP2.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism of impaired neurotransmitter release due to mutations in INS and VAMP2 could lead to the development of targeted therapies that aim to restore or compensate for deficits in neurotransmission, potentially benefiting patients with both conditions.

#### 7. Griscelli syndrome type 2  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.389)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-264876)

**Proposed mechanism:** INS (HGNC:6091) —DISRUPTS→ Insulin Secretion (P00016); Insulin Secretion (P00016) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes Mellitus (HP:0000821); RAB27A (HGNC:9781) —DISRUPTS→ Melanosome Maturation and Trafficking (GO:0001723); Melanosome Maturation and Trafficking (GO:0001723) —LEADS_TO→ Hypopigmentation (HP:0001005); RAB27A (HGNC:9781) —DISRUPTS→ Cytotoxic Granule Exocytosis (GO:0031100); Cytotoxic Granule Exocytosis (GO:0031100) —LEADS_TO→ Immunodeficiency (HP:0002711). Loss-of-function mutations in INS impair insulin secretion leading to diabetes (MONDO:0013240). Concurrently, loss-of-function mutations in RAB27A disrupt melanosome maturation and trafficking, as well as cytotoxic granule exocytosis, leading to hypopigmentation and immunodeficiency characteristic of Griscelli syndrome type 2 (MONDO:0011872). The shared mechanism lies in the disruption of distinct cellular trafficking pathways by mutations in genes encoding key proteins (INS and RAB27A) involved in vesicle formation and transport, albeit with different downstream consequences.

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of pathogenic variants in RAB27A in patients diagnosed with MONDO:0013240 or pathogenic variants in INS in patients diagnosed with Griscelli syndrome type 2, without other identifiable genetic causes. _(variant: None specified for hypothetical INS-related rare disease; for RAB27A, variants associated with Griscelli syndrome type 2 are typically rare and damaging, thus unlikely to be present at high frequency in gnomAD.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanistic principle of disrupted intracellular trafficking, despite different causal genes and primary pathways, could reveal common therapeutic targets or strategies for managing cellular dysfunction in these rare diseases. For example, if specific protein degradation pathways are affected, interventions targeting these might be beneficial across both conditions.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared pathway of proinsulin processing, despite distinct causal genes, could reveal novel therapeutic targets for metabolic and neurological disorders. Strategies aimed at enhancing or restoring the efficiency of this pathway might offer benefits for patients with either Wolfram syndrome 1 or BDV syndrome, or related conditions.
